My body has two sides

Place your hands on the table. Do they appear similar? Can you identify any differences between them?

Reflection 1: Looking closely

If you place one hand on top of the other, do they match perfectly? Try it and think about what makes them similar and what makes them different.

Left handRight hand

text.imgdesc: The figure shows a person's two hands raised with all fingers extended, each pointing toward a fruit.

text.text: Now, bring your hands together with palms facing and examine your fingers. Do they possess identical sizes? What about your hands—are they also of the same size?

Although your two hands look very much alike, they are not exactly the same. Your left hand is a mirror image of your right hand. If you place one hand against a mirror, it looks like the other hand. This special kind of sameness, where one side is a mirror copy of the other, is called symmetry.

Reflection 2: Mirror images

Hold your right hand up to a mirror. Does the reflection look like your left hand or your right hand? What does this tell you about how the two hands are related?

Drawing

Fold a piece of paper in half. Place your left hand on one side and trace its outline with a pencil. Once completed, repeat the process with your right hand on the other side.
Left handRight hand

Now look at your two drawings side by side. Notice how the outline of the left hand and the outline of the right hand face opposite directions, yet they have the same shape and size. If you cut out one drawing and flip it over, it would match the other. This is another way to observe symmetry in your own body.

Reflection 3: Comparing drawings

If you fold the paper along the middle line, do the two hand outlines overlap? Why or why not?

My body

Next, take a look at your arms. Do they exhibit similar features? How about your legs? Can you observe they are equal, where one side of your body mirrors the other? Compare with your friend or teacher to see if they also have equal sides.

Our bodies have an imaginary line running down the middle, from the top of our head to the ground. This line divides us into two halves—a left side and a right side. Each half has one eye, one ear, one arm, and one leg. This arrangement, where the left side mirrors the right side, is called bilateral symmetry. The word bilateral simply means two sides.

Reflection 4: Two sides of the body

Stand in front of a friend. Is the left side of your friend's face the same as the right side? Can you find small differences? What might cause those differences?

Conclusion and practice

Our bodies are unique, with symmetrical sides. And we're not alone—many other organisms exhibit similar symmetry. Explore leaves of plants and observe other animals to confirm their symmetrical features.

In this lesson, we learned that our bodies have bilateral symmetry—the left side is a mirror image of the right side. We discovered this by observing our hands, tracing their outlines, and examining our arms and legs. Symmetry is not only found in humans: butterflies, leaves, and many other living things also display it. The next time you look at an animal or a plant, try to find the imaginary line that divides it into two matching halves.

Reflection 5: Symmetry around us

Look at a butterfly, a leaf, or your own face in a photograph. Can you draw the imaginary line of symmetry? Are the two halves perfectly identical, or are there small differences?

exercise_v2.question: If you place your left hand against a mirror, does the reflection look like your right hand?
exercise_v2.additionalInfo: The reflection of the left hand in a mirror looks like the right hand because our hands are mirror images of each other. This is an example of bilateral symmetry.

exercise_v2.question: Are the two sides of a human body perfectly identical?
exercise_v2.additionalInfo: Although the left and right sides of our body are very similar, they are not perfectly identical. Small differences exist, such as in fingerprints, birthmarks, or the way we use one hand more than the other.

exercise_v2.question: Is bilateral symmetry found only in humans?
exercise_v2.additionalInfo: Bilateral symmetry is found in many living things, including butterflies, fish, dogs, and even some leaves. It means that one side of the body is a mirror image of the other.
